question: What is the main goal of a Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in a public hospital?

options.A: To fund free medical care for all citizens indefinitely
options.B: To generate large commercial profits for hospital expansion
options.C: To replace the national health ministry budget entirely
options.D: To guarantee a steady, continuous supply of essential medicines

explanation: Spot on! The whole point of a DRF is to make sure the pharmacy never runs out of crucial drugs by using a self-replenishing pool of money. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why does money collected from selling drugs in a DRF go right back into the fund instead of a general government account?

options.A: To ensure the money is immediately available to buy more drug stock
options.B: To pay off international government debts and loans
options.C: To cover the cost of unrelated building construction projects
options.D: To pay the personal salaries of the hospital management team

explanation: You got it! Keeping the money right where it is (ring-fencing it) ensures the pharmacy can restock quickly without waiting for government bureaucracy. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h1)

question: What do we call the starting money or initial drug stock used to launch a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: The initial money or drug stock used to start the fund
options.B: The monthly profit withdrawn by the hospital accountant
options.C: The fine paid by patients who lose their drug prescriptions
options.D: The emergency tax collected from private pharmacies

explanation: Exactly! 'Seed capital' is just the starting push—the initial cash or drugs needed to get the revolving cycle rolling before patient payments start coming in. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h2)

question: What is most likely to happen if a new DRF launches with too little seed capital?

options.A: Patients will receive completely free medications for life
options.B: The government will stop taxing local pharmaceutical companies
options.C: The pharmacy will experience immediate stock-outs due to low inventory
options.D: The facility will automatically make massive profits in the first week

explanation: Spot on! If you start with too little inventory, you can't meet patient needs, and the system stalls before it even really begins. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h2)

question: Where does an established DRF get most of its ongoing income?

options.A: Fines collected from healthcare workers who arrive late
options.B: Annual gifts from international sports organizations
options.C: Direct monthly donations from private manufacturing companies
options.D: Out-of-pocket user payments from patients buying drugs

explanation: Correct! Every time patients pay for their prescriptions, that money goes right back into keeping the fund alive and well. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h3)

question: How do daily patient payments keep the Drug Revolving Fund alive over time?

options.A: They build new residential quarters for the hospital nursing staff
options.B: They fund overseas training trips for senior medical doctors
options.C: They replace the money spent on inventory so new drugs can be bought
options.D: They pay for the electricity bills of the entire hospital complex

explanation: You got it! Patient payments replace the cash spent on the last batch of drugs, funding the very next order. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which of these is NOT a benefit of bringing health insurance into the DRF model?

options.A: It provides a secondary stream of income for purchasing drugs
options.B: It helps spread healthcare financial risks across a larger population
options.C: It completely eliminates the need for any initial seed capital
options.D: It protects patients from paying high cash prices out of pocket

explanation: Correct! Insurance brings in great ongoing funds, but you still need that initial stock or cash to get the pharmacy doors open in the first place. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h4)

question: A hospital pharmacy is full of drugs, but the DRF has no cash because an insurance partner is six months late paying claims. What is this called?
explanation: Spot on! When the money is trapped outside the hospital waiting on delayed payments, cash flow gets choked up, leaving you unable to place new orders. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why can relying completely on international donors be risky for a hospital's Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: International agencies refuse to supply common medicines like antibiotics
options.B: Donor drugs are always expired before they arrive at the hospital
options.C: Local nurses are legally forbidden from handling donated medical items
options.D: Donor programs can end or shift priorities abruptly, causing shortages

explanation: Right! External aid can disappear overnight. If you don't have a local system making money to buy drugs, you'll run out fast when donors leave. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h5)

question: A clinic gets a large free donation of malaria drugs. To best support the long-term DRF, what should management do?

options.A: Dispense them properly and capture revenue or track stock to build replacement reserves
options.B: Give all the donated medicines away for free without keeping any pharmacy records
options.C: Sell the donated items to private retail pharmacies for personal staff profit
options.D: Hide the drugs in a secure warehouse and wait for local prices to increase

explanation: Great thinking! Treating donations responsibly and tracking every item helps build a sustainable local stock cushion before the free meds run out. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h5)

question: What are 'retained earnings' in a Drug Revolving Fund?

options.A: Modest operational surpluses kept within the fund to buy more stock or upgrade facilities
options.B: Cash bonuses distributed directly to the personal bank accounts of doctors
options.C: Penalties paid by patients who fail to return their empty drug bottles
options.D: Special taxes collected by the government from private drug importers

explanation: Spot on! These are the extra savings made from good management that stay inside the fund to fight inflation and improve patient care. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h6)

question: What happens to a DRF if its extra cash is constantly pulled out to fund unrelated hospital projects?

options.A: The cost of purchasing medicines from wholesale vendors will drop
options.B: Patient satisfaction scores will rise due to improved hospital buildings
options.C: The pharmacy will automatically attract more international donors
options.D: The fund will eventually collapse and fail to restock essential drugs

explanation: Correct! If you drain the pharmacy's working capital for other things, you won't have enough cash left to replace sold medications when prices go up. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h6)

question: Which factor is most important for keeping a DRF cycle running successfully for years?

options.A: Strict financial discipline and accurate inventory monitoring
options.B: Relying exclusively on large, unpredictable international donations
options.C: Stopping all forms of health insurance participation in the hospital
options.D: Selling all essential medicines at extremely high commercial markups

explanation: You got it! Good bookkeeping, careful stock checks, and making sure money always finds its way back to inventory are the real keys to success. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h7)

question: A ward nurse notices some liquid medicines are close to expiring. What action best protects the DRF?

options.A: Report the expiring stock promptly so it can be redistributed or used before expiration
options.B: Throw the bottles into the regular municipal trash can without telling anyone
options.C: Take the medicine home to treat family members privately without a prescription
options.D: Hide the expiring medication at the back of the shelf until it spoils completely

explanation: Spot on, nurse! Catching near-expiry drugs early allows you to move them to busy wards so they get used up instead of turning into financial waste. [learn more](GNS215_U3_T2#GNS215_U3_T2_h7)
